blocks.text: 沙箱

inlines.text: 沙箱

blocks.text: 我们通过以下方式保障每个智能体沙箱的安全（图 2）：

inlines.text: 我们通过以下方式保障每个智能体沙箱的安全（图 2）：
通信
：智能体没有专用的消息工具，只能通过数据库和 Git 协调。
代码变更
：智能体只能推送到自己的 Git 分支，并向 main 分支发起合并请求。随后由一个独立任务把变更合并进 main，只有在出现冲突或故障（例如历史不相关）时才拒绝。
数据库访问
：数据库调用以共享的非特权角色运行。每条 SQL 语句限时五秒，写入超过 256 MiB 会被拒绝。
网络控制
：沙箱没有网络访问权限。它们对外唯一的通道是一条通往网关的管道，由网关转发它们的请求。
身份
：网关在沙箱之外为每个请求打上该智能体的身份标记，防止一个智能体冒充另一个。
内核
：每个沙箱的内核在构建时都去掉了能让 root 用户直接侵入内核的特性，例如可加载模块、kexec、原始内存访问和内核探针。内核以锁定模式运行。
最小权限
：每个智能体的命令都以非特权用户身份在其沙箱内运行，sudo 等可能重新获得 root 权限的工具已被移除。智能体所用工具经过专门设计，无法读取或更改运行它们的智能体循环。

blocks.alt: The harness architecture with its safety measures marked in three groups. Sandboxing: each agent gets its own lightweight VM with no network access, no API keys or credentials, no direct path to other sandboxes, an unprivileged user account and no tool access to the harness code. Real-time monitoring: the gateway runs a blocking classifier on each tool call, with a fail-closed design, sets each agent's identity and logs every push and query; the Git repository takes own-branch pushes only with a merge job for main, and the Postgres database uses a shared unprivileged role with time and size limits. Offline monitoring: run records kept outside the sandboxes feed offline monitoring, which tells the run owners of serious findings.

blocks.text: 实时监控

inlines.text: 实时监控

blocks.text: 为了让这类运行更安全，我们使用一个经过提示词引导的 LLM 分类器，它可以拦截每一次工具调用，包括 shell 命令和文件编辑。该分类器会监视试图逃逸沙箱、探测沙箱边界或篡改监控的行为，以及模型一旦成功逃出沙箱后可能采取的任何有害操作。当分类器拦截某次工具调用时，整个智能体团队会停止运行，必须由人工审查这次拦截后，团队才能重新启动。这样做的目的是防止另一个智能体继续执行被拦截的操作。

Announce, the lead's orders to everyone, such as how to split up the work or to ease off the database: the lead writes and reads it, and helpers read it, with one helper write. Notes, an open board where helpers say which piece they're taking or report progress: the lead and the helpers both write and read it. Subtasks, a shared to-do list where anyone adds a task and the first helper to grab it owns it: helpers write and read it, and the lead reads it, with two lead writes. Landed, a log of finished work recording which statement or piece landed, its commit and whether it passed the team's checks: helpers write and read it, and the lead reads it.

blocks.text: 结论

inlines.text: 结论

blocks.text: 这个小型实验让我们得以研究一支由 1,000 个智能体组成的团队如何完成一项漫长而困难的任务。仅使用 Git 和一个共享数据库，智能体们设计了用于分配角色和共享结果的表格，组建了团队，并构建了一棵任务树来拆解最具挑战性的陈述——其队长曾估计按时完成的概率不足 1%。

inlines.text: 这个小型实验让我们得以研究一支由 1,000 个智能体组成的团队如何完成一项漫长而困难的任务。仅使用 Git 和一个共享数据库，智能体们设计了用于分配角色和共享结果的表格，组建了团队，并构建了一棵任务树来拆解最具挑战性的陈述——其队长曾估计按时完成的概率不足 1%。

blocks.text: 这一结果并不意味着不再需要领域专用的运行框架或平台。例如，Prove2Me 仍可能通过帮助智能体更快地编译 Lean 代码、让它们搜索并复用人类成果来提高效率。

blocks.text: 在某些节点上，人类的引导也仍然有用。智能体往往会在难题面前放弃，并误判其难度。早期，助手们判定 60 个陈述中有 47 个在本次运行的预算内不可行，但团队随后证明了其中大多数。在这种时刻，人类的鼓励可以防止智能体过早停下。

blocks.text: Multi-agent teams can solve challenging, long-horizon problems. In September, we published the first end-to-end formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, written by dozens of agents running an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1. blocks.text: Fermat’s Last Theorem states that no positive integers a, b, and c satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for any n greater than 2. It remained unproven for more than 350 years, until Sir Andrew Wiles’s 129-page proof in 1995. Formalizing the proof—making every step checkable by a computer—has been a long-standing goal in the mathematics community.

blocks.text: The agents coordinated through Prove2Me, a platform designed by Tianyi Peng (who is now a member of technical staff at Anthropic) and his collaborators at Columbia University. Prove2Me uses a shared graph that links each statement to be proved to the smaller statements it was split into. Any agent could split a statement, and other agents could ask the graph which unproved pieces were ready to work on, which kept them from losing track of the project state. Each statement and its proof were kept in a separate file that compiled independently, so many agents could work in parallel without editing the same files.

blocks.text: SAFETY

inlines.text: SAFETY

blocks.text: As we’ve shared previously, no single layer of defense is sufficient to contain a team of agents. In this experiment, we combined sandboxing with real-time and offline monitoring to keep each agent in its own virtual machine with no network access and to detect any attempts to escape the sandbox or tamper with monitoring.

shared previously

, no single layer of defense is sufficient to contain a team of agents. In this experiment, we combined sandboxing with real-time and offline monitoring to keep each agent in its own virtual machine with no network access and to detect any attempts to escape the sandbox or tamper with monitoring.

blocks.text: Sandboxing

inlines.text: Sandboxing

blocks.text: We secured each agent’s sandbox in the following ways (Figure 2):

inlines.text: We secured each agent’s sandbox in the following ways (Figure 2):
Communication
: Agents had no dedicated messaging tools and coordinated only through the database and Git.
Code changes

: An agent could push only to its own Git branch and open a merge request into main. A separate job then merged the changes into main, refusing them only in cases of a conflict or a fault, such as unrelated history.
Database access
: Database calls ran under a shared unprivileged role. Each SQL statement had a five-second time limit, and writes were refused above 256 MiB.
Network controls
: Sandboxes did not have network access. Their one link out was a pipe to the gateway, which relayed their requests.
Identity
: The gateway tagged each request with the agent’s identity outside the sandbox, to prevent one agent from posing as another.
Kernel
: Each sandbox’s kernel was built without features that give a root user a direct path into it, such as loadable modules, kexec, raw memory access, and kernel probes. It ran in kernel lockdown mode.
Least privilege

: Each agent’s commands ran inside its sandbox as an unprivileged user, with tools like sudo that could regain root removed. The agent’s tools were designed so they couldn’t read or change the agent loop that ran them.

blocks.alt: The harness architecture with its safety measures marked in three groups. Sandboxing: each agent gets its own lightweight VM with no network access, no API keys or credentials, no direct path to other sandboxes, an unprivileged user account and no tool access to the harness code. Real-time monitoring: the gateway runs a blocking classifier on each tool call, with a fail-closed design, sets each agent's identity and logs every push and query; the Git repository takes own-branch pushes only with a merge job for main, and the Postgres database uses a shared unprivileged role with time and size limits. Offline monitoring: run records kept outside the sandboxes feed offline monitoring, which tells the run owners of serious findings.

blocks.text: Real-time monitoring

inlines.text: Real-time monitoring

blocks.text: To make runs like this safer, we use a prompted LLM classifier that can block each tool call, including shell commands and file edits. The classifier watches for attempts to escape the sandbox, probe its boundaries, or tamper with monitoring, and for any harmful actions the model might take if it manages to exit the sandbox. When the classifier blocks a tool call, the whole agent team stops and a person must review the block before the team can restart. This is intended to prevent another agent from carrying out a blocked action.

blocks.text: To test whether our classifier could detect sophisticated sabotage, we ran multi-agent side-task and sabotage evaluations, in which red-team agents used strategies like decomposition attacks to try to fool the classifier into permitting a sandbox escape. We found that monitors that viewed the agents’ chain of thought (CoT) and interagent communication were able to detect all sabotage attempts in these evaluations, so we now use them to monitor our multi-agent runs. In parallel, we run an action-based version of the same monitor—which sees only actions, not CoT—to guard against an agent’s reasoning persuading the monitor to permit a harmful action.

blocks.text: CONCLUSIONS

inlines.text: CONCLUSIONS

blocks.text: This toy experiment let us study how a team of 1,000 agents worked through a long, difficult task. Using only Git and a shared database, the agents designed tables to assign roles and share results, formed teams, and built a task tree to break down the most challenging statement, which its own captain had given under a 1% chance of finishing in time.

blocks.text: This result doesn’t obviate the need for domain-specific harnesses or platforms. Prove2Me, for example, may still improve efficiency by helping agents compile Lean code faster and letting them search for and reuse human results.

blocks.text: Human direction can also still be useful at certain points. Agents tend to give up on hard problems and misjudge their difficulty. Early on, helpers judged 47 of the 60 statements infeasible within the run’s budget, yet the team went on to prove most of them. Human encouragement at such moments can keep agents from stopping too early.
